identity.title: Ability to stand and walk unaided (truncal ataxia grade; inability = central marker)

technique.how: With an assistant ready, ask the patient to sit unsupported, then stand, then walk a few metres. Grade truncal/gait instability: 0 = normal; 1 = mild sway but walks unaided; 2 = walks only with support/one-sided assistance; 3 = cannot stand or walk even with support (or cannot sit without arm support). If the patient cannot get up, note whether they can sit still unassisted.
technique.prerequisites: Adequate blood pressure and no orthostatic symptoms; assistant present for fall prevention. Compare with baseline mobility in elderly or frail patients.
technique.contraindications: Do not attempt to stand a hypotensive, actively vomiting or obtunded patient; use the sitting test instead.

interpretation.positive_finding: Grade 3 instability (cannot stand or walk unaided) in acute vertigo is almost exclusively central - pooled specificity about 99% (LR+ high), and 0/25 peripheral patients in Kattah 2009. Grade 2-3 instability is more sensitive (71-81% pooled) but less specific (83%).
interpretation.negative_finding: Walking unaided does not exclude posterior-circulation stroke: grade 3 instability is present in only about 36-44% of central AVS, so a patient who can walk still needs HINTS and imaging assessment when indicated.
interpretation.pitfalls: Peripheral vestibular neuritis causes unsteadiness (grade 1-2) that is easily over-called, especially in the elderly, the intoxicated or those with prior neuropathy; sedatives, Wernicke encephalopathy and alcohol withdrawal also produce ataxia. Grading systems differ (Lee 2006 vs Moon 2009), which changes sensitivity.
interpretation.changes_what: Cannot stand/walk unaided (grade 3): treat as central; stroke work-up regardless of HINTS. Walks unaided: lowers but does not remove need for HINTS; still image if other red flags.

estimates.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome (stroke or other central lesion) - severe (grade 3) gait/truncal instability
estimates.population: Pooled AVS cohorts (10 study cohorts, n=800; stroke and vestibular neuritis)
estimates.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
estimates.quote: Severe (grade 3) gait/truncal instability had high specificity 99.2% (95% CI = 97.8-100.0) but low sensitivity 35.8% (95% CI = 5.2-66.5).

estimates.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome - grade 2 or 3 gait/truncal instability
estimates.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
estimates.quote: highest for a normal hHIT (79.9% [95% CI 72.2-87.5]), grade 2 or 3 gait/truncal instability (80.8% [45.1-100.0])
estimates.location: Results, 'Diagnostic accuracy of bedside examination findings' (Ann Neurol 2023;94:295; PMC10524166); supplementary Table 2

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of acute prolonged vertigo/imbalance - grade 2/3 graded gait/truncal instability (GTI)
estimates.population: 18 studies, 1025 patients with acute vestibular syndrome (665 ischemic strokes, 306 acute unilateral vestibulopathy)
estimates.quote: Grade 2/3 GTI had moderate sensitivity (70.8% [95% confidence-interval (CI) = 59.3-82.3%]) and specificity (82.7 [71.6-93.8%]) for predicting a central cause

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of acute prolonged vertigo/imbalance - grade 3 GTI (cannot stand/walk unaided)
estimates.quote: grade 3 GTI had a lower sensitivity (44.0% [34.3-53.7%] and higher specificity (99.1% [98.0-100.0%]).

estimates.target_condition: AICA/PICA-territory stroke vs vestibular neuritis - grade 2-3 truncal ataxia (including inability to sit still as substitute)
estimates.population: 52 prospectively studied AVS patients (stroke and vestibular neuritis)
estimates.quote: grade 2-3 ataxia to differentiate patients with vestibular neuritis from patients with stroke resulted in a 92% sensitivity (95% CI 79-100%), a 67% specificity

estimates.target_condition: Ischemic stroke in AVS - severe truncal ataxia (cannot sit unassisted)
estimates.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (69 ischemic strokes vs 25 peripheral) at a stroke referral center
estimates.reference_standard: MRI (or CT) for stroke; normal MRI plus clinical follow-up for peripheral

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not stand hypotensive, vomiting or obtunded patients; interpret with caution in patients with baseline gait impairment (neuropathy, parkinsonism, prior stroke, intoxication) where inability to walk is not new.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: New inability to stand or walk unaided with acute vertigo is a central sign until proven otherwise, even with a normal CT and a peripheral-appearing HINTS; Carmona 2023 found truncal ataxia without nystagmus in 15% of acute-vertigo patients, mostly strokes.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Sensitivity differs by grading scheme used (Lee 2006 grade 2/3: 73.8% vs Moon 2009: 57.4%, p=0.001, Cerebellum 2024); no kappa data identified. Grade 3 (cannot stand) is the most reproducible cut-off.

extraction_notes: Two pooled sources (Ann Neurol 2023 via PMC full text; Cerebellum 2024 via abstract) give grade-3 and grade-2/3 estimates separately; they overlap in included studies but use different pools and are reported separately, not averaged. Ann Neurol 2023 grade-2/3 specificity is in its supplementary Table 2, which I could not view, so it is null. Kattah 2022 (abstract) reports grade 2-3 ataxia sens/spec for stroke vs neuritis with MRI standard. Kattah 2009 Table 4 values read from PMC full text (severe truncal ataxia = inability to sit without arm support). Tarnutzer 2011 CMAJ (anchor) has abstract-only PMC deposit, so cited without numbers; Carmona 2023 cited for the ataxia-without-nystagmus caveat (15% of cohort, abstract).
